To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Lys-substitued gramicidin analogs form nonselective pores in lipid membranes and erythrocyte membranes.
lysine-substituted derivatives of gramicicin A are able to form pores in lipid bilayer membranes, which results in leakage of liposomes and erythrocyte lysis.

the Lys-substitution of gramicidins A and its analogs leads to the loss of ion channel-forming ability, but the resulting peptides are able to form nonselective membrane pores, which can be detected in liposomes, in planar bilayers and in intact erythrocytes, but not in artificial planar bilayers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of pore formation by Lys-subtituted gA analog, which is a promising candidate for the design of novel antimicrobial agents.
a novel type of membrane-permeabilizing peptides that are capable of forming large pores in model and natural membranes.
the effect of the position of a charged residue on the biological activity of gA and its derivatives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the introduction of a positively charged lysine residue into the N-terminal position of gA is a promising approach to obtain an ion channel inhibitor, whereas the lysine residue introduced in the C-terminal position of the peptide has a detrimental effect on the selectivity of the channel.
the Lys-substitution at the N-termini of gA is a prerequisite for pore formation, whereas Glu-substitution is not sufficient for pore formation.

the Lys-substitution of gA at the N-terminal position is more effective in inducing membrane leakage than the Glu-substitution at the same position, whereas the Lys-substitutions at positions 2-6 are less potent in this respect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a charged group near either the C- or N-terminus is able to restrict dimerization of gA and suppress its channel activity, but the N-terminal lysine derivative is able to form nonselective pores

a charged group near N-terminus is not necessarily an obstacle to the formation of ion-conductive pores by gA, but it may rather facilitate oligomerization of the peptide in the membrane, leading to formation of a nonselective pore.
introduction of a positively charged amino acid residue in the vicinity of the N-termini of gA results in a peptide that is capable of forming giant pores in lipid bilayers and erythrocyte membranes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the introduction of the lysine group into gA at the N-termini of the peptide chain is not sufficient to suppress the ability of gA to form nonselective ion channels in lipid membranes.
the presence of a charged group near one terminus of gA is not a sufficient condition for the peptide to be inactive.
the introduction of the charged amino acid residue into the N-terminal position of gA results in a significant loss in its channel-forming ability and a gain of its pore-forming ability.
